title: World Englishes — A Pluricentric Language

pts: The World Englishes framework describes global English as a pluricentric language with multiple, legitimate national and regional varieties.
Kachru's Three Circles model distinguishes Inner Circle (native-speaker-majority), Outer Circle (institutionalised second-language) and Expanding Circle (foreign-language) contexts.
This directly extends Unit 24's brief introduction and Unit 59's critical standard-language-ideology work into a full descriptive framework.
points.who: Braj Kachru's Three Circles of English model

v: A large drawing of Kachru’s circles; country cards

items: Draw three concentric circles and label them Inner, Outer and Expanding.
In groups, place country cards (India, UK, Singapore, Germany, Nigeria, Japan, USA, Kenya, Brazil) in the circles.
Discuss cases that are hard to place: Singapore, where many children now grow up with English at home; South Africa; the Netherlands.
Place your own class: where do your learners’ Englishes belong?
Discuss the model’s strengths and limitations.
Learners draw their personal ‘circles’ of English contacts: family, school, media, online friends.
Support: provide one fact about English in each country on the card.
Challenge: read a short summary of criticisms of the model and propose an improvement.

lines: India: Outer Circle. But a child in a Bengaluru apartment may use English at home with parents, which looks like the Inner Circle.
Singapore: Outer Circle officially, but English is the main home language of many families today.
Netherlands: Expanding Circle, yet English is used widely in universities and business.

blocks.x: The model describes national history well; it describes individual speakers less well. Schneider (2007) offers a developmental model of how postcolonial Englishes gain their own identity over time.

body: Purpose: to show Kachru’s model and its fuzziness. Content: three concentric circles with example countries; dotted arrows show movement (e.g. Singapore towards the centre); the edges are shaded rather than sharp. Style: clean diagram. Board version: three circles with country names.

items: Google Earth (free) to locate countries and discuss the spread of English.

blocks.x: Chalk circles on the floor or board, and handwritten country cards.

points.h: English as a Lingua Franca, Formalised
pts: English as a Lingua Franca research studies English used specifically among non-native speakers, as its own legitimate linguistic system, not a deficient approximation of native norms.
This directly extends the Lingua Franca Core (Unit 4) into a fuller sociolinguistic and pedagogical research programme.
ELF interactions often show mutual accommodation strategies and systematic simplifications that function perfectly well communicatively.
points.who: Jennifer Jenkins, Barbara Seidlhofer's ELF research

v: A recording or transcript of an interaction between two non-native speakers

items: Play or read a short conversation between, for example, an Indian and a German engineer.
Learners note any moments of misunderstanding and how they were resolved.
Groups list strategies: repeating, rephrasing, checking, simplifying, using a shared technical term.
Learners compare with the repair strategies in Unit 30.
In pairs, learners role-play a similar exchange and deliberately use two of the strategies.
Learners who have online contacts abroad (games, forums) collect examples of successful ELF communication.
Support: provide a strategy checklist to tick while listening.
Challenge: learners compare an ELF exchange with an Inner Circle exchange and discuss which is easier to understand, and why.

lines: A: The machine is giving a vibration at high speed.
B: A vibration… you mean shaking? Shaking at high speed?
A: Yes, yes, shaking. From the motor side.
B: OK, from the motor. We check the bearing first.
A: Bearing first, then balance.

blocks.x: Neither speaker uses a native-speaker form throughout (‘is giving a vibration’, ‘we check’), yet the exchange succeeds through repetition and checking. Seidlhofer (2011) found such accommodation typical of ELF talk.

body: Purpose: to show ELF accommodation. Content: two speakers on either side of a gap, each adding planks labelled ‘repeat’, ‘rephrase’, ‘check’, ‘simplify’ until the bridge meets in the middle. Style: friendly. Board version: two figures and a bridge with labels.

items: Audacity (free, open source) to edit short recorded exchanges.

blocks.x: The teacher and a colleague read the transcript aloud.

pts: Choosing a target variety (British, American, or a more ELF-oriented model) is a genuine pedagogical decision, not a neutral default.
This connects to Unit 2's needs analysis — the right choice depends substantially on learners' actual likely contexts of use.
Many contemporary courses now explicitly teach awareness of variation rather than a single variety as the only correct model.

v: Needs analysis notes (Unit 2) for two different classes

items: Take two classes with different futures, for example a Class 9 group in a rural school and an adult group preparing for work in the Gulf.
For each, list who learners are likely to speak English with and in what situations.
Decide a target model for production: British, American, an educated Indian model, or an ELF-oriented model.
Decide what varieties learners should recognize.
Write a short justification for each decision.
Trainee teachers each defend a different choice in a short panel discussion.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Class 9, rural Karnataka: most English use will be with other Indians and in exams. Production model: educated Indian English, clearly intelligible. Recognition: British and American media voices.

Adult group, Gulf hospitality work: English with guests from many countries and colleagues from South and South-East Asia. Production model: ELF-oriented, focused on intelligibility. Recognition: Arabic-, Filipino- and Russian-influenced Englishes.

blocks.x: The choice is not neutral. Many coursebooks default to one Inner Circle variety, but the right model depends on learners’ likely contexts of use.

body: Purpose: to show variety choice as a decision. Content: a signpost with arms labelled ‘British’, ‘American’, ‘Indian’, ‘Lingua franca’; beneath it, two learner profiles with arrows to different arms. Style: clear. Board version: a signpost with four arms.

items: Google Forms (free) for a learner survey on future English use.

blocks.x: A paper survey with three questions: With whom? Where? For what?

pts: Expose learners to multiple varieties' vocabulary, pronunciation and idiom differences, building recognition even while focusing production on one target variety.
This connects to Unit 32's extensive listening — varied authentic audio naturally builds this receptive variety awareness over time.
The goal is comprehension flexibility across varieties, not necessarily productive mastery of more than one.

v: 30 minutes per week for four weeks
Short audio clips of speakers from several countries

items: Each week, play three short clips (30–60 seconds) of speakers from different circles talking about the same topic.
Learners answer the same simple comprehension questions for each clip.
They note one feature that surprised them (a sound, a word, a phrase).
Keep a class chart of varieties heard.
After four weeks, learners report which varieties became easier to understand.
Link the tour to extensive listening (Unit 32): learners choose one clip a week to follow up independently.
Support: provide transcripts for the first listening.
Challenge: learners identify the country of origin and explain what helped them decide, avoiding stereotypes.

lines: Nigeria: the speaker said ‘I’m coming’ when he was leaving the room for a minute.
Scotland: the ‘r’ in ‘work’ was strong, like in Kannada.
Singapore: the speaker said ‘Can or not?’ at the end of a question.

blocks.x: The aim is comprehension across varieties, not productive mastery of several. Learners focus their own speech on one intelligible model while learning to understand many.

body: Purpose: to show receptive variety awareness. Content: a world map with small speech bubbles at several points, each with a headphone icon; a learner with headphones at the centre. Style: bright, inclusive. Board version: a rough map with dots.

items: International Dialects of English Archive (IDEA) (free) for recordings of many varieties [VERIFY current access].
YouTube (free) interviews and talks from speakers in several countries.

blocks.x: The teacher and colleagues from different regions record short clips on a phone; or read transcripts aloud.

body: Some usages widely associated with Indian English, such as prepone (to bring forward in time), are now recorded in major English dictionaries. Checking current dictionary entries is a useful classroom activity [VERIFY entries in current editions].

pts: Extend Unit 24's cultural materials audit to variety representation specifically — which Englishes do a coursebook's voices and settings represent?
Global coursebooks have historically skewed heavily toward Inner Circle varieties and settings, though this is gradually shifting.
Supplementing with Outer and Expanding Circle authentic materials builds a more genuinely representative linguistic picture.

items: For one coursebook unit, list every speaker and setting (listening, reading, pictures).
Classify each by circle and by variety.
Count the proportions.
Compare with your learners’ likely contexts of use (point 3).
Choose two supplementary materials that add Outer or Expanding Circle voices.
Learners audit a unit themselves and suggest additions.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Speakers: 7 British, 2 American, 1 Australian. Settings: London café, New York office, Sydney beach.
Missing: any Indian, African or Asian speaker; any setting in which English is used between non-native speakers.
Supplements: an interview with an Indian scientist; a short story by a Nigerian writer (in a graded version, Unit 31).

blocks.x: Global coursebooks have historically concentrated on Inner Circle voices, though this is gradually changing. The audit extends the cultural materials audit of Unit 24 to varieties.

body: Purpose: to show representation in materials. Content: an open coursebook with small figures stepping out of its pages, each labelled with a country; a bar chart beside it shows the proportions by circle. Style: clean infographic. Board version: a simple bar chart.

items: Google Sheets (free) for tallying and a quick chart.

blocks.x: A tally chart in the teaching journal.

pts: A learner using a non-Inner-Circle but internally consistent and effective variety raises real questions for assessment criteria built around a single standard.
This connects to Unit 46's rubric design — intelligibility and communicative effectiveness (Unit 4's Lingua Franca Core) may be more defensible criteria than strict conformity to one variety.
This remains a genuinely unresolved, actively debated area within language testing more broadly.

v: Three learner recordings or scripts; your speaking rubric (Unit 46)

items: Review your speaking rubric. Does any criterion reward similarity to a native-speaker model (for example, ‘native-like pronunciation’)?
Rewrite such criteria in terms of intelligibility, effectiveness and appropriacy to the task.
Score three learner performances with both versions.
Discuss any learner whose score changes.
Decide which version to use, and note unresolved questions.
Invite listeners from outside the school to rate intelligibility, and compare with teacher scores.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Before: ‘Pronunciation is close to a native speaker.’
After: ‘Pronunciation is clear enough for listeners from different backgrounds to understand without strain; key sounds from the Lingua Franca Core are produced consistently.’

blocks.x: A learner’s script says Kindly do the needful and revert by Monday. Under a British-standard rubric this is marked as unidiomatic; under an effectiveness rubric for an Indian workplace email it is clear and appropriate, though the teacher may point out that international readers may find revert confusing. Canagarajah (2006) argued that assessment should give more weight to strategies for negotiating varieties. How to assess such performances in high-stakes tests remains actively debated (Unit 73).

body: Purpose: to show variety-aware criteria. Content: three stacked cards reading ‘Is it intelligible?’, ‘Is it effective?’, ‘Is it appropriate here?’; a crossed-out fourth card reads ‘Is it native-like?’. Style: clear, bold typography. Board version: three questions written large.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared, revised rubric.

blocks.x: The revised rubric on chart paper in the staff room.

pts: Recognising World Englishes validates learners in Outer Circle contexts who may already speak an institutionalised, legitimate local variety of English.
This connects to Unit 59's critical awareness and Unit 72's identity discussion — variety choice carries real identity weight for many learners.
This isn't an argument against teaching a specific target variety where learners want or need one — it's an argument against treating other varieties as simply wrong.

v: A short text in Indian English (written for this book); a British or American parallel

items: Learners read two short texts on the same topic, one in Indian English and one in British English.
They find differences in vocabulary, grammar and style.
They discuss: which is ‘correct’? Correct for whom, and where?
They sort differences into ‘fine anywhere’, ‘fine in India, may confuse elsewhere’, ‘error in any variety’.
Learners write a short note explaining one Indian English expression to an international friend.
Learners collect Indian English expressions from newspapers and advertisements over a week.
Support: provide the differences highlighted; learners sort them.
Challenge: learners discuss when they would choose one form or the other.

lines: ‘My cousin-brother is coming’ → fine in India, may confuse elsewhere; ‘my cousin’ works internationally.
‘The meeting is preponed’ → widely understood in India; ‘brought forward’ works internationally.
‘He don’t know’ → nonstandard in educated Indian and British English alike.

blocks.x: Learners who already speak an Indian variety are not speaking wrong English. They are learning to move between local and international settings, which is a valuable skill. Variety choice carries identity weight (Unit 72), and teaching a target variety is fine where learners want or need it; what matters is not treating other varieties as simply wrong.

body: Purpose: to show movement between local and international English. Content: a road sign pointing one way to ‘Local’ (a Bengaluru street scene) and the other to ‘International’ (an airport), with a learner confidently choosing a direction. Style: warm, positive. Board version: a two-way arrow with labels.

items: Online dictionaries such as the Oxford Learner’s Dictionaries (free) and Cambridge Dictionary (free) to check how usages are labelled.

blocks.x: A class wall chart with two columns: ‘In India we say…’ and ‘Internationally we can also say…’.

points.sub: What this changes day to day
pts: Most classroom practice doesn't need wholesale change — it needs conscious awareness that the variety being taught is one legitimate choice among several, not the only correct English.
This closes the loop with Unit 4's Lingua Franca Core, Unit 24's intercultural competence, and Unit 59's critical awareness, now unified into one coherent sociolinguistic picture.
Tier IV will return to this territory with deeper theoretical and research grounding.

body: For the next month, add one short listening clip a week from a speaker outside the Inner Circle. At the end of the month, ask learners which clip they understood best and which surprised them, and note any change in their confidence.

dek: Unit 74 of 100: closing this stretch of Tier III by treating global English variety as the genuine norm to teach toward, not a set of deviations from one fixed standard.

aims.x: English is now used by far more people who learned it as an additional language than by people who grew up with it. It has many centres: London and New York, but also Delhi, Lagos, Singapore and Manila. This unit treats that variety as the normal condition of English, not as a set of deviations from one correct standard. It draws together earlier threads on the Lingua Franca Core (Unit 4), intercultural competence (Unit 24) and critical language awareness (Unit 59), and it suggests what, in practice, should change in an ordinary classroom.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain the World Englishes paradigm and Kachru’s Three Circles model, with its limitations;
describe English as a Lingua Franca research and its classroom implications;
make and justify a choice of target variety for a particular group of learners;
build learners’ receptive awareness of several varieties;
audit materials for the varieties they represent;
design assessment criteria that value intelligibility and effectiveness;
respond respectfully to learners who already speak an Indian variety of English;
summarize what a World Englishes perspective changes in day-to-day teaching.

why: Why this matters. English has no single owner or centre anymore. Teaching it as if it did leaves most learners underprepared for the actual global English they'll encounter and use.

background.x: Braj Kachru, a linguist from Kashmir who worked in the United States, argued from the 1970s that English had become a pluricentric language, with legitimate varieties developing their own norms. His Three Circles model (Kachru 1985) distinguished the Inner Circle, where English is the primary language of most people (the UK, the USA, Australia); the Outer Circle, where English was established during colonial rule and has institutional functions (India, Nigeria, Singapore); and the Expanding Circle, where English is learned as a foreign language (China, Brazil, Japan). Kachru’s The Indianization of English (1983) described Indian English as a variety in its own right. The model has been criticized for tying varieties to nations and for overlooking the variation within each country (Schneider 2007), but it remains a useful starting point.

A second research programme examines English as a Lingua Franca (ELF): English used between speakers who do not share a first language, most of whom are not native speakers. Jennifer Jenkins (2000) proposed the Lingua Franca Core, a set of pronunciation features most important for international intelligibility (Unit 4). Barbara Seidlhofer (2011) showed that ELF interactions follow their own regularities, with speakers accommodating to one another and adjusting their language to make meaning clear. Andy Kirkpatrick (2007) described the pedagogical implications, including what he calls a lingua franca approach for contexts such as ASEAN.

Indian English has been described in detail, with its own features of pronunciation, vocabulary, grammar and discourse (Sailaja 2009). Its speakers include judges, novelists, engineers and scientists. For teachers, this raises practical questions. Which variety should we model? Should prepone or cousin-brother be corrected? How should a test score a learner who says I am having a doubt? The answers are not always simple, but they should be made consciously, with learners’ needs in view (Unit 2), rather than by default.

NCF 2023 emphasizes communicative competence and learners’ confidence in using English (NCERT 2023). A World Englishes perspective supports both. Part IV returns to this territory with deeper theoretical and research grounding in Unit 78 and Unit 96.

items: Variety decision. A justified choice of production and recognition models for one class, based on needs analysis.
Materials audit. A coursebook unit audit with proportions by circle and two supplementary materials.
Rubric revision. A speaking or writing criterion rewritten around intelligibility and effectiveness, tested on three samples.
Learner task. Learners’ sorting of Indian and international expressions, with a short explanatory note.
Which variety of English did you learn as ‘correct’? How has your view changed?
How do you respond when a learner uses an Indian English form such as prepone?
Whose voices do your learners hear most in class? Whose do they rarely hear?
Does any of your assessment criteria reward native-likeness rather than intelligibility?
How would you explain your choice of target variety to parents?
How does your own English shape your identity as a teacher?

terms.def: (1) An adjustment to how a learner accesses a task or test, such as extra time or enlarged print, which changes the route but not the destination. (2) In ELF talk, adjusting one’s speech to be understood by a listener.

English used as a shared language between speakers who have different first languages, such as an Indian and a Japanese engineer. Research focuses on mutual intelligibility rather than conformity to native-speaker norms (Seidlhofer 2011).
In Kachru’s model of World Englishes, countries where English has no historical or official role but is widely learned as a foreign language, such as China, Japan and Brazil (Kachru 1985).
The variety of English used in India, with its own features of pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar, such as prepone or co-brother. It is a legitimate variety of English in its own right.
In Kachru’s model of World Englishes, countries where English is the primary language of most people, such as the UK, the USA and Australia (Kachru 1985).
The extent to which a speaker’s words can be understood by listeners. Many teachers now aim for international intelligibility rather than a native-speaker accent (Jenkins 2000).

In Kachru’s (1985) model of world Englishes, the countries, such as India, Nigeria and Singapore, where English was established through colonial history and has official or institutional roles alongside other languages.
A language with several interacting centres, each providing a national variety with its own norms, as English has in Britain, the USA, India and elsewhere.

Kachru’s model of English worldwide, with the Inner Circle (e.g. the UK), the Outer Circle where English is a second or official language (e.g. India) and the Expanding Circle (e.g. China) (Kachru 1985).

The varieties of English used around the world, such as Indian, Nigerian and Singaporean English, each seen as legitimate with its own norms. The concept is closely associated with Kachru’s Three Circles model.
